一篇写给老矿工的失望记录 你一开始点开《异动核心》的时候，其实是带着一点期待的。 不是那种“哇新游戏来了”的期待，而是那种很熟悉的感觉—— 像是听到老同事又回矿洞了，装备还是那一套，啤酒还是那个味，你知道接下来会发生什么：挖矿、打虫、指着金矿和蘑菇互相发癫，然后喊着 Rock and Stone 收工回家。 可惜，这次你下去之后，第一铲子就觉得不对劲。 一开始你还以为只是“前期弱”。 武器没改装，伤害低一点正常；节奏慢一点，也能理解。 但很快你就发现，这不是成长问题，这是规则变了。 以前你是带着一套完整的职业体系下矿的： 你知道自己能干什么，队友能干什么，四个人凑在一起是一个精密的小机器。 但现在不是。 现在你开局像个被扒光了装备的临时工，能不能打、怎么打，全看这一局系统给你发什么。 你捡到什么强化，你才是什么职业。 那一刻其实挺微妙的—— 你不是在“玩一个熟悉的职业”，你是在“赌一个能不能成型的build”。 问题就从这里开始慢慢积累。 你会遇到那种局： 强化全是边角料，武器打不动，虫子一波一波压上来，你一边后退一边意识到，这局游戏其实在几分钟前就已经输了，甚至可能在开局拿到的第一把武器时就该意识到，只是系统还没通知你。 也会遇到另一种局： 强化刚好契合，输出爆炸，一路平推。 听起来挺爽对吧？ 但多玩几把你就会发现—— 这两种体验的差距，大到不像同一个游戏。 原来的《深岩银河》不是这样的。 它的乐趣在于：你们四个人怎么通过默契的配合，把一场本来很艰难的任务努力的“打赢”。 而现在的乐趣变成了： 系统这把愿不愿意让你赢。 你开始怀念一些很具体的东西。 怀念工程师把平台一块块铺出来的安全感， 怀念钻机一头扎进地里开出一条逃生路线， 怀念侦察兵那一发照明弹，把整个洞穴点亮。 那些东西不是数值，是一种很难被替代的“可控性”。 也是在这个时候，很多老玩家开始说出那句最关键的话： 这游戏，好像灵魂不见了。 原作里最让人上头的，其实不是枪有多强，也不是怪有多难。 而是那种—— 你可以随便拿钻头乱挖、垂直乱飞、把整座洞穴炸成蜂窝煤的自由劲儿。 下班了，和朋友一起下去晃悠。 边挖边聊，偶尔被虫子追得鸡飞狗跳，最后满载而归唱着歌回家。 那种感觉，很松弛，很解压。 可《Rogue Core》不是这样。 它的地图开始变得更“规整”了。 你能明显感觉到关卡被设计过——多了很多工业设施，多了走廊和平台，少了那种天然洞穴的野性。 你还是在地下，但不再是在“一个可以被你改造的空间”里了。 地形破坏还在，但乐趣被削弱了； 垂直探索还在，但意义变少了。 取而代之的，是另一种东西： 时间压力。 现在的每一局，更像是被皮鞭甩在身上的赶工。 45分钟到50分钟一趟，中间几乎没有喘气的空间。 你不是在“探索”，你是在“推进”。 再加上基础难度本来就不低—— 单人玩起来很吃力， 匹配队友又经常不稳定。 于是体验慢慢发生变化： 从一开始的 “哈哈哈新游戏真开心”， 变成了后来的 “呼……好累啊。” 再往后，你会开始注意到那个本该很好玩的系统——构筑。 每一局从零开始，捡强化、拼build，这本来是Rogue最核心的乐趣。 但问题在于，它给你的东西不太对。 你拿到的很多升级是这样的： 伤害+5%、弹夹+2、冷却缩短一点点。 它们不是没用，只是—— 太干了。 没有那种“哦这下要起飞了”的瞬间， 也很难拼出那种离谱到破坏平衡的强力组合。 更尴尬的是，你们还得共用升级站。 于是你会看到队友来回跑、互相等、甚至有点“抢”的感觉。 节奏一下子被打断，合作反而变得别扭。 再看局外。 你本来以为，既然局内是重置的，那局外应该有足够强的成长来兜底。 但现实是： 局外成长很薄弱，内容一眼望到头。 你刷着刷着，会开始觉得重复、觉得只是单纯的流水线操作， 却又没有一个很明确的“我在变强”的反馈。 玩到这里，其实很多老玩家心里已经有答案了。 他们不会说一大堆设计术语，只会摇摇头说一句： “这哪是深岩银河啊。” 甚至有人说得更直接一点： “这就是个披着矮人皮的快节奏硬核射击游戏。” 如果只看这些问题，其实还可以解释成一句话： 这是一个方向不一样的游戏。 但它偏偏又撞上了另一个现实—— 它现在是EA。 于是那些本来就敏感的地方，被进一步放大： 匹配偶尔抽风， 偶尔会有bug， 偶尔来点小崩溃， 内容还不够撑得住长时间游玩， 后期重复感来得很快。 如果这是一个全新IP，大家可能会再等等。 但它不是。 它叫“深岩银河”。 于是最后那点情绪，就落在了一个很现实的地方： 价格108，新玩家可能觉得还行。 但那些冲着原作来的老矿工，很难不失望。 有人甚至会忍不住说一句： “你们干脆给原作做个新模式多好，非要单独卖个新游戏？” 你玩到最后，其实已经不太生气了。 你知道它不是没想法， 也不是不用心， 甚至偶尔还能看到一点——如果它成了，会很好玩的影子。 但问题是： 它现在给你的，不是你当初想回来的那个地方。 最后一句话 它不是把菜做糊了。 它是端上来一盘完全不同的菜， 却还用着原来的菜单。

我是岩神1400小时的萌新，以一个客观的角度来评价。 游戏底子很好，其实还是好玩的。老登们有能力的可以尝试玩玩看，萌新就别来受苦了。 目前问题： 一价格：首先你作为一个EA阶段的半成品，首发价格来到了惊人的108，如果加上支持包就是150+的价格。 对比隔壁刚出的尖塔和西土。 你一没尖塔有那么多的玩家基础，二没西土持续将近两周的首发打折。 而且从内容量来看，这个价格已经可以算得上非常昂贵了。 很难想这个体量是你鬼船用了三年搞出来的东西。 二界面UI： 部分词条没有完全翻译，人物语音也会丢失。 选择服务器把五湖四海各个国家的房间都推在一起，想要找个国服房间比登天还难。 游戏结束阶段通关好歹做个通关动画吧？ 干什么，把精英团队直接留地底下不要了？ 三难度方面： 这一代有伪逃杀机制加快游戏进程，在一个初期不熟悉任务机制，且技能不解锁完全的情况下，游戏难度直线飙升。 每推进一关卡还得选个令人血压升高的DEBUFF词条。 多人还好，上限摆在这里。但是单双人你就玩吧，一玩一个不吱声。 而且粪怪及其多，在随机武器池子的影响下你开局不好更是做大牢。 四游戏机制： 作为主打肉鸽类型的合作游戏，你这池子太浅了，武器池和人物池占一个强化设施极其愚蠢。 武器照搬原版，光加数值不加机制。升级奖励来来回回就那么几个东西。 但，最大问题的就是——以‘团队’为名义让四个人共同在一个池子里选择奖励。 就算往好处想，大家都团结友爱互相谦让。 一个人从奖励里5选1和四个人从奖励里按照先后顺序5选4。 是头猪都知道哪个游玩体验更好吧？ 在公用的池子里，想要不牺牲个人的游玩体验根本不可能有爽感。 最终的结果就是注定要牺牲个人的体验来成全其他人。 隔壁西土就因为这事被吐槽好多次了，但人家听劝马上就改成独立卡池了。 不改这一点，真的迟早要完。 五游玩过程体验： 老岩神是可以中途加入房间的。但是本作你只能在第一关卡中加入或者重连。 如果你的队伍在第二关卡中有人掉线/退出的话，那么你整局游戏的队友位永久—1 照目前游戏难度来说，你再怎么牛逼也做不到老岩神那样一拖二/三的。 而且我是想不明白，为什么血量和护盾是分开计算的？ 你说想增加难度我能理解，但在我有护盾的情况下还同时扣血量是什么意思？ 目前的资源在难3以上根本不够用。 敌人的难度增加你好歹也把矮人们的能力稍微增加下吧。 老岩神有侦察和枪手以及钢铁这种兜底能力。 你们有啥？是第五强大的死了就直接查无此人的回溯还是每秒恢复1点护甲的技能？ 老岩神每个职业特色分明，每个人都有自己专门负责的事情，那叫团队协作。 这五个职业除了技能不同以外，我是不清楚团队在哪了 而且游戏流程实在是太长了，平均几乎40分钟一把游戏。 如果玩的爽也就算了，玩的还不爽。 那我干嘛花钱找虐，加点钱去隔壁超级地球好歹还能爽一爽吧。 首发这游戏的基本都是岩神玩家，而且是期待你鬼船新作，且愿意为你买单的人。 从当前的情况来看，只能说吃相真的太难看了。 希望你们听劝，好好整改，毕竟是EA，还有挽救的余地。 不要让老矿工们伤心。

我今天找到了《深岩银河:异动核心》的续作《深岩银河》😊😊😊，玩了几个小时，感觉比异动核心好玩多了🥰🥰🥰。 这一作移除了肉鸽属性，简直神来之笔🤩🤩🤩，把肉鸽配装的随机不可控改为了武器和被动的加点，让玩家在玩法搭配上有更多的自主权💪💪💪，这种想玩什么玩什么还不用和队友抢的感觉真的很棒👍👍👍。 护甲机制也有大改，虽然护甲值大削😑😑😑，但是快速可恢复护甲让游戏有了更多容错🤗🤗🤗。补给不仅补充弹药还补充血量了，再也不会因为缺少回血手段暴毙了🤤🤤🤤。 职业分配也更好了👷♀️👩🌾🧑🔬👩🍳，虽然限制了职业的武器和道具，但是大大加强了矮人的合作配合🤝🤝🤝，大家一起打怪挖矿完成任务一起rock&stone真的是太棒了☝☝☝，再也没有了肉鸽抢加点只能有一两个人爽的分歧问题👎👎👎。 计时器也取消了😽😽😽，任务时间更加宽松，有老东西愿意花二三十分钟给我讲任务该怎么做，氛围真的是太好了😭😭😭。以前因为有任务计时器，任务时间很赶，每次都被任务进度推着走，蛮不适应的😤😤😤，这作真的很棒。 敌人设计超越前作。这作的敌人不再是难以瞄准的吗喽🐒🐒🐒，而是改成了虫子🐛🐛🐛，不仅造型可爱而且移速很慢😇😇😇，对新手很友好。敌人护甲机制比前作更加优秀，敌人的护甲可破坏这一点对游戏的影响更加明显，把虫子的护甲打掉看它们裸奔真的很有趣。boss机制也不错，和玩家的互动很强，不像前作异动核心全是超雄，攻击性拉满🤬🤬🤬。 《异动核心》的续作《深岩银河》游玩体验真的很好，我想我应该能玩一千六百多小时吧😻😻😻

Solo 无装备已碾压D4，准备尝试一些奇怪的构筑和打法。一般不给抢先体验版游戏打差评，所以默认好评。 难度个人觉得还好，第一层的前三抓的确很重要，但拿不到关键组件也不至于会难到没法玩。在DRG里积累的部分经验能在一定程度上降低理解成本，但完全拿DRG的思路来往RC身上套明显是行不通的。 目前的合作模式对于野队而言确实是个大问题，但作为大部分时间都在玩solo的独狼需要考虑的自然也就没那么多了，反倒是升级选项缺乏职业辨识度和构筑多样性的问题在我看来要更致命一些。另外生物强化模组的内容也有些过于局限了，现阶段只能替换其他职业的固定卡组显然是远远不够的，最好的方案是能在卡池里加入更多选项然后允许玩家自由进行局外搭配。 至于局外强化内容我认为得彻底推倒重做，目前的这套纯数值体系对角色功能性的影响微乎其微，这种通过削减玩家数值然后在局外一点点补回来以平衡难度曲线的设计很难称得上高明。 我应该还会继续玩上一段时间，至少会打完EA的白金，希望一年之后这游戏能迎来质的飞跃吧。

I'm going to have to disagree with the naysayers on this one. The DRG Rogue Core Early Access experience is a bit unrefined, but every new patch brings it closer to an extremely satisfying roguelite shooter. In this review, I'll try to break down the most common critiques I've seen across other reviews. To be fair, many of these critiques are [b]perfectly valid[/b] but I don't quite find them to be so prominent as to ruin the overall experience. This will be the sentiment expressed throughout this review. Now, for the critiques: [h2]The Timer[/h2] In Rogue Core, every depth has a timer - upon reaching 0, the team must endure an endless swarm until they escape to the next depth. After the initial learning curve, I realized that with an average team of reasonably experienced dwarves, we could easily adapt to the timer and figure out how we need to allocate our time without micromanaging. Upgrade negotiations pause the timer, offering a reprieve to assess and strategize. Sometimes we would get down to the wire but it was usually because we made a daring choice to complete a sub-event before extracting. These choices are often result in heart pounding situations where the monstrosities creeping in from the walls nip at our butt cheeks as we leap desperately through the elevator doors to the next hellscape. Was it worth it? Upgrades always help, I suppose. But was it fun? [i]Absolutely.[/i] Since its EA release, the Rogue Core devs have allowed you to customize the timer to your liking to be more relaxed if you want to, well... relax. They have also made it more clear when swarms are set to arrive with plans to improve upon the timer's design in future patches. However, I would disagree with those who want the timer to disappear completely - the timer is what sets Rogue Core apart from its predecessor. The timer is your [i]true[/i] enemy. It forces you to think in terms of balancing risk with reward. It compels you to communicate with your team. It keeps you from dawdling too long in one place. And most importantly, it forces your team into some truly exhilarating skirmishes that push you to your limits. That being said, if you were looking for a comfortable balance of ups and downs that DRG Classic provides, you won't find it here and that can be jarring for sure. But I suspect this time-based gameplay loop will appeal to some folks who might be coming hot off of their last Risk of Rain gauntlet. [h2]The Negotiations[/h2] Again, I loved the core idea behind negotiations! In Rogue Core, all players periodically huddle up to select upgrades from a limited pool. Each person takes a turn to select but you are able to mark your favorites out of turn if you see something you really like. The big complaint here was that the first player(s) would take the good stuff leaving others with scraps. However, I've found that in a perfectly selfish game, whoever's first always picks the "best" all purpose upgrade. However, because first choice rotates, they never get the synergies necessary to make it into a functioning meta build. Everyone loses. However, everything changes when communication is involved from the get go. Having the conversation early on to establish your roles/affinities make it so that negotiations aren't ever an issue. I'm no expert on every class but just having touched the Guardian and Slicer classes myself, I've noticed some distinctive affinities for a few different play styles. For example, slicer can operate as either a distractor/tank or an extremely potent close range melee character (pickaxe hits got a huge buff from DRG Classic!) Guardian can just as easily play around stuns and area control as it can with AOE damage and explosions. With a little up front communication and ongoing discussion, you can establish each player's personal meta so that the team never steps on each other's toes. This results in some games where [i]everyone[/i] is pulling off some truly devastating combos and making keen use of some of the lesser utilized upgrade effects. The other complaint is that there aren't enough potent effects to provide unique synergies. On this, [b]we agree[/b]. While I definitely have made some broken builds through my runs, I find myself gravitating to those builds time and time again, depending on other players' roles. The upgrade diversity could use some work and the devs need not fear creating swingier rare upgrades that change your playstyle much like unstable overclocks did in DRG Classic. However, I trust that this is something that will evolve dramatically as the game moves through early access. The synergies that do exist [i]work[/i] and feel [i]good[/i] so I know the devs are putting thought and care into each upgrade. All they have to do now is to season the upgrade pool with a fair bit of zest. Finally, the devs have made some seriously nice improvements since EA release, responding almost directly to suggestions that I've made along with much of the community. Offered upgrades in a round of selections are now always of the same rarity. Selected upgrades are always replaced with another of the same rarity. And rarities themselves, along with upgrade effects, are being balanced in every new patch. This has quelled many of my personal gripes against this system and I suspect many of the earlier negative reviewers might appreciate them as well. [h2]The Progression[/h2] This is where my complaints align with the community. I do [b]not[/b] feel very rewarded for being a longer term player. DRG Classic handles this with a balance of overclocks and cosmetics that are still offered 100s of hours deep. Rogue Core offers a progression tree with unlockable modifiers you can assign your starting build. These modifiers are fairly bland, including basic stat buffs like: more health, pickaxe damage, elemental resistance, etc. I'm only a few hours in and I've already made it past the halfway point of this progression tree. From here, the tree only offers upgrades to the nodes I've already selected. I doubt it will take me all that long to fill this tree out completely. The clearance system ensures that new mechanics trickle in for a little while, but that too whittles down very quickly and offers very little. Rogue Core is missing one of the quintessential aspects of rogue likes/lites that keep people coming back - game changing unlocks. I'm talking new weapons added to your pool, modified/upgraded class abilities, unlocked sub-classes, the return of overclocks, stronger starting buffs or risk/reward tradeoffs. These unlocks need to dramatically change the way you approach the game to be successful. I have a sneaking suspicion (and hope) that there is [b]much[/b] more planned for the future to keep players engaged. However, as long as the gameplay itself is fun, I'll keep playing. Naturally, that brings me to the last segment: [h2]The Good[/h2] DRG Rogue Core isn't perfect but I've had an utter blast playing it. In addition to the praises I gave for the admittedly underbaked negotiation and timer systems, the gunplay is as strong as ever. The DRG core is still there and is bolstered by a number of satisfying new weapons and mechanics to play around with. One of the newer weapons introduced in a recent patch, the Trident, is now one of my favorite weapons in DRG history. The gameplay itself feels frantic and varied. The core spawn are far more aggressive and move with a chaotic energy - I no longer feel I can control a rampant swarm on my own if my teammates go down. Many have claimed this is a bad thing. However, I think, as a rogue like, [i]this is expected.[/i] You are expected to die if you aren't locked in. You [i]will[/i] feel the disappointment of defeat. But, when I do bro down with a solid team, you better believe we're standing our ground, taking some names, and [b]reclaiming what's ours.[/b] ROCK AND STONE

As an original DRG player who purchased it in early access when the only class was the Gunner and the sole mission type was Morkite mining to see it get to where it is now. I have the utmost faith in Ghostship Games to get this on track. Bearing that in mind, I can't recommend Rogue Core in it's current state. Core gameplay loop - much it feels and looks like DRG, but the rogue-like/lite elements are just implemented poorly in my opinion that makes for a lot of Hurry-up and Wait; usually that waiting is on other players for your lobby. While the cire gameplay loop also doesn't feel like you can be successful in runs if you're playing solo as either the ammo economy or sheer number of enemy spawns will become the barriers. In that the Rogue-like/lite elements that are huge detriments are actually the upgrade menu feels competitive rather than cooperative with how the skills are done. Admittedly improvements were attempted on this menu but what I've found is getting rid of the wait mechanic for everyone to meet up around the resource carrier bot didn't get rid of the human sabotage elements. Then menu will give a series of 3-5 upgrades depending on the number of players but then have you sit in a queue for when you can select an upgrade. Thee is a button to effectively claim dibs on an upgrade, but that doesn't prevent another player for sniping it before you get your turn which then recycles that card to some other ability that may be less desirable depending on what you're trying to do. This is also another one of those hurry up and wait mechanics as this upgrade menu gives a 30 second timer to each player and some folks take that whole time even if you've decided on what you wanted immediately. I've made the suggestion to copy Spell Brigade where the upgrade menus are bespoke for each player and the wait would only occur if someone doesn't make all of their selections quickly. Further Hurry-up and Wait occurs when you get to the critical weapon or equipment boxes for when you're in the first armory or at the deeper levels as Both Equipment and a Heavy Weapons crate are options for choosing a path down from level to level. Which requires all players to be present otherwise it won't even open the selection menu. If you have someone that went off in a different direction it's a huge time sink to wait for them to get back to activate those that adds to a different frustration with other players. I'll admit I'm also guilty of passing those crates at times because the levels are not also defined important side focuses are compared to the cable for the golden path. And as the gameplay loop is a race against the clock to the elevator to get down to that next level passing things up is very easy to do. Timer - you're racing against this thing and it doesn't give you a lot of information like when you're going to experience a large wave of spawns or major events until the very end which then pulls all the breaks off spawn restrictions and just looks to overwhelm you. I wish I had more ideas as to how to correct this, but I really think the system works, where it isn't working is that the routes off the golden path can sometimes be quite long and consume too much time. Or the events you find a long the way often consume too much time. So there are other areas to simplify things that could correct the problems here. Weapon Balance is poor, often it feels like you're expending too many rounds for the basic chaff enemies you have in the experience. This is sometimes corrected as you come across work benches and select upgrades for your weapons, but if you stick with just one weapon you'll run into more ammo economy issues and be perpetually out of ammo. Even when you get a second weapon it just stretches things out a little bit but then they both don't really put down targets well. Much of this could be addressed with a full balance pass and equate out a specific minimum standard for damage. I'd probably do this as a baseline DPS for all the weapons and readjust all the stats based on optimum play for each weapons unique mechanics so that uniqueness is still there while the effectiveness should feel better for everyone. Class abilities for the characters, these are just not made equally. I've played each of the classes and tried the primary and secondaries for each of these class abilities and found them wanting across the board. I'll be fair and say I don't like class abilities like that in any game really be it Overwatch, Destiny, or this. I think class abilities trying to be the defining factor is uninteresting means to do things. As classes are locked to 1 person as a class pure lobby if someone else has selected the class you want then you're forced to take another one that you may not like. This is just a poor user experience ontop of class abilities that may or may not feel worthwhile. Really the only one I like is the Spotter which has a dart that once applied allows everyone shooting that target to have critical hits for 10 seconds. The rest just don't feel like they matter much. Character progression feels and looks terrible. If you're unlocking cosmetics its a flat grid that then you click on a tile and have a submenu popup asking for what class to apply that option to. The options in this menu mostly don't matter or look good so you're not encouraged to make use of it compared to the shop with more options for resources from DRG or driving toward stuff in the Seasonal Battlepasses for DRG. This just may be a lack of content at this point, but if that were the case just get rid of the menu and put them in the cosmetic boxes located in dives at various depths. The menu itself doesn't feel good right now. Challenges to unlock the currency for unlocking items is in a menu that's not readily accessible while in mission or looking at the mission board, so you're constantly having to move back and forth to double check things. The passives for all the characters are unlocked on a single menu, but to put those passives on a character you need to unlock the slots (max of 6) to then apply them. And the passives are not all made equal - there are some that just don't seem worthwhile in the current systems to use at all. While I've thrown this all into a Review, I've also used the survey system that is presented to player to also give all this feedback. Ghost Ship can likely fix all these complaints in time, I just want to make sure people know the experience right now is most likely to be negative until a lot of refinement goes into place to polish these things out...and that may be awhile.

I play co-op games weekly with group of friends (4 of us), and we've definitely enjoyed it so far. I've had a bunch of fun, rewarding & challenging gameplay. However, I did read critical reviews beforehand. So I went in knowing (and having told my mates) that the focus is on rolling with the punches with what you get, and making quick decisions on how much to bite off given the time pressure (and less so about exploration) -- despite the game not communicating these things well to a new player. I really like these focuses: for weekly gaming sessions, being forced to play differently each time keeps things fresh. Also how the gun system works means my pre-game loadout is super simple. I don't need to ever worry about re-jigging my loadout before my mates wanna start the next run if I'm getting bored! The building time pressure also means runs in Rogue Core typically go much faster than my team's runs in DRG's equivalently epic Deep Dives: either you keep pace, or you die [i]([b]or[/b] someone pulls off something amazing!)[/i] We did really enjoy Deep Dives, but kept putting off doing them 'cos we didn't know if we'd finish by the end of the night's session. Despite whatever impression the game gives you when you first start playing it, be ready to act fast, and make risk/reward decisions on trying side quests, weighing up whether the reward is worth the time sink and the extra difficulty that'll come with that. My group has both played lots of DRG, and various roguelikes. So we no doubt had those DRG expectations & familiarity with most of the gameplay mechanics. But we've also enjoyed co-op games with procedural generation, where the fun is you've gotta work out what to do with what the game throws at you, like Plate Up, Unrailed, Out of Space, Neon Chrome, and Space Lines from the Far Out. Plate Up has a similar mechanic where the group has to pick between two cards, each with a random extra challenge & also extra reward. And at least one other where you make a new character build each run from randomly given choices, like 9 Parchments (we played on Switch, so you won't see my playtime for that). I'd like to point out it is explained perfectly in-universe why these elite soldiers are going in with no shields and no weapons, with "The Grayout Barrier" (it's even mentioned on the store page). This like, [i]the[/i] central conceit for justifying the games roguelike mechanics (at least within the DRG universe), they should probably emphasise it a lot more, especially in the marketing ('cos that's basically the communication a player gets from the company before buying the game). If you don't have a group of friends to play with, I can't speak to the experience of playing this game with strangers, as I haven't done that at all. If you're coming from a similar perspective as we did, and or are willing to try out a faster paced, roll-with-the-punches game, you'll very likely also have a blast.

I have around 1,000 hours in the original Deep Rock Galactic on another Steam account. I played on the highest difficulties, both solo and with other players, so I know what I like about DRG and what I expect from a game in this universe. I had around 28 hours in the Rogue Core playtest and alpha version. I played it before release, including a test about six months before launch. In the release version, I played for about 1 hour and refunded the game, because I quickly realized that it was almost the same thing I had already seen in the alpha. Yes, the developers added some visual improvements. The station looks better, there are more details, and the game looks a bit more polished. But I care about the gameplay, not the station. And the gameplay still feels boring, repetitive, and weak. Rogue Core tries to be a roguelike, but it does not have enough real variety. The perks are not interesting. They do not feel strong or meaningful, and they do not make me want to try different builds. After a few runs, everything starts to feel the same. Similar rooms, similar fights, similar pacing, similar missions. There is procedural generation, but it does not make the game feel fresh. This is especially disappointing when compared to the original Deep Rock Galactic. The original DRG feels more varied, more alive, and much more fun to replay. It has better biomes, more memorable situations, and more reasons to come back. Rogue Core is supposed to be a new game in the DRG universe, but right now it feels smaller, weaker, and less interesting. The price makes it worse. Asking around 30 dollars for the game in its current state feels too much. What makes it even stranger is that during the Steam Summer Sale 2026, the developers did not offer any discount at all. Even a small discount would have shown that they understand the current state of the game and want more players to try it and give feedback. But there was no discount. The only positive thing I can mention is the cooperative player base. The people I played with mostly knew what they were doing. But I think this is because the active player base is small, so the people who still play are mostly the ones who already enjoy the game. The problem is that even with good teammates, I still did not have fun with the game itself. I am very disappointed. The original Deep Rock Galactic was one of my favorite games, and I spent more time in it than in almost any other game. Rogue Core does not feel like a worthy next step for DRG. It feels like an expensive, unfinished, and repetitive experiment that was sold too early. I do not recommend it in its current state. After 28 hours in the playtest and 1 hour in the release version, it is clear to me that the most important part, the gameplay, has barely changed. Maybe the game will become better after several major updates, but right now, for 30 dollars, it is a very weak offer.

While it has been improved, this game still [b]fails to justify itself as a standalone game that costs just as much as DRG[/b]. It's not like it isn't enjoyable, but most of what's enjoyable about it is the enjoyable stuff that was already present in regular old DRG, and it lacks the replay value or longevity of DRG once you're done unlocking stuff. [b]The attempt at rogue-like elements adds very little to DRG's formula[/b], at least in the way it was done here. For one thing, for being called "Rogue" Core, and being billed as a roguelite, it's barely any more Rogue-like than DRG already was (and DRG is certainly not a rogueli(ke/te)); the most meaningful "Rogue-like" elements present in Rogue Core are procedurally generated levels, and having to start the mission over, probably with a new seed, if you die. These are both already features of DRG. You might say that the level generation is a little more Rogue-like in Rogue Core because there are distinct floors, but this just doesn't bring much to the table other than the missions being longer. The change to the formula otherwise to make it a "roguelite" is only to add "pick from 4 upgrades" screens (which is really Slay the Spire/Survivors mechanics, and largely unrelated to Rogue-like design, despite the current trend of calling a game a "roguelike" when you really mean "deckbuilder"), and to randomize your starting loadout, which doesn't really make it any more or less rogue-like considering that even pure, traditional roguelikes have consistent starting gear for each class. And there's a good reason that those games have you start with certain gear and attributes and try to build into what your character is good at rather than picking up anything you see, instead of being purely games of grabbing every random thing you see with no build agency. It doesn't bring any of the things that are interesting about roguelikes or roguelites to DRG, and it doesn't really bring anything interesting to the table in general, but rather, mainly just amounts to having a less interesting kit even at the end of a run than any character in DRG can have to start with. After all, the classes in DRG have more thoughtful kits with planned out synergy, while in Rogue Core you just have a grab bag of ♥♥♥♥. The randomization of elements that were symbiotic in DRG also means there is much less class interaction because you can't count on it, contributing again to it being a less interesting DRG (quite a shame because DRG had a successful co-op formula, which is not an easy thing to create, and with this game threw it out). And the game is easy enough that developing a well synergized kit is just not necessary to win. In fact, it's hardly necessary to engage with the expenite upgrades or kit RNG at all to win, because the most consistent strategy is just using the guaranteed resources in every level, the workbenches and bio-boosters, for upgrading your characters' innate abilities. Your Slicer doesn't really need to worry about whether his gun can kill the boss quickly when his slice ability has 5 stacks of eclipse system and 5 damage upgrades, Falconer scarcely needs to worry about her guns or ammo when she can easily be upgraded so that you can just mindlessly keep sending out the attack drone to shred everything on your behalf, Guardian isn't worried about getting hit when he can constantly spam fear effects (a strategy so broken that even players of modded difficulties don't run the fear mod on the coil gun in DRG because it trivializes the game so much), and so on. Which brings me to my next point: [b]The game very quickly becomes completely rote.[/b] Rush workbenches and bio boosters, take whatever grab bag of expenite upgrades you roll, and unless you skipped all the work benches and got completely terrible RNG, shred the boss's health bar in like 5 seconds every phase. I thought before release that it would be nice if they were leaning more into the movement shooter aspects of DRG. That even does seem to be how it's billed. Technically a lot of actions are faster at base (although many cancels have been significantly nerfed, so it's debatable if you're truly faster than you can be in DRG), and the Reclaimers are presented as elites who are more combat-ready than the mining crews of regular DRG. But in practice I find that the game often feels slower and less responsive. Only one class, Slicer, has a traversal ability as part of its base kit. Using a pickaxe halts your speed and momentum. Falling causes you to be locked into an obnoxious, lengthy landing animation, making Cushion IV mandatory on everyone except maybe Slicer because the fall height to trigger this is aggravatingly low. I hardly get the impression that the Reclaimers are as elite or combat-ready as the game tells me when I remember that every member of the supposedly weaker mining crews of regular DRG has access to Dash. The way the "Q" press state for using class abilities work is also pretty unresponsive and clunky. According to GSG this game started out as a new game mode for DRG. Had it only been that, I think it would just be inoffensive and a neat little diversion, if perhaps a very uneconomical and bloated addition to the game. But as a standalone game that costs as much as the main game it doesn't pull its own weight, or really offer any positive qualities not already offered by DRG.

Nothing you get in the runs feels like it matters at all. Absolutely zero dopamine release ever. The only defining difference between whether you succeed or fail is purely mechanical Deep Rock skill. The builds don't ever matter enough to swing you from having to sweat to getting to be OP and stomp things, neither does getting a bad build actually hinder you from being able to just play the game slightly more optimally and get it done regardless. I don't think there's a single thing I've been excited to acquire as an upgrade aside from like... maybe the artifact? And even that is like... the bare minimum power bump I would expect from a roguelite run upgrade. It'd be one thing if you got a ton of upgrades over the course of the game but it's very stingy. You get 4 bio-boosts, 4 weapon crates, and some misc extra things for each depth. Having a half decent build is entirely reliant on getting at least 4 different upgrades to synergize (and be a good fit for your weapon + class) to even feel like you have a "thing" going on. So by the time you're most of the way through you feel like you only just got your build online (and it'll be something super exciting like "have a decent crit chance but only on Tuesdays" + "critting enemies stuns them for a couple seconds" *RIVETING*) and then at that point the only thing you can really take that feels relevant is either more crit chance or longer stun so it feels like you've already done all the interesting stuff as soon as it starts doing anything. There's no cool end of build capstone that makes it feel powerful, everything is fed to you in tiny increments 4-5 minutes apart from each other MINIMUM. I've never had roguelite run progression feel so utterly agonizing. Nothing like spending a solid minute or two of precious slipping time trying to find that last bit of Expenite to get an upgrade only for it to be a common roll and you might as well just take the extra HP. Also Classes still don't feel quite there. The increase from 1 class ability to 3 was a great change (seriously though what were they thinking with classes only having 1 thing they do that never changes lol), I like the abilities themselves but the bio-boosters and the build variety needs a rework. Why is the Falconer basically forced to do some kind of electric synergy? Two of her three abilities and basically all her bio-booster deck upgrades revolve around electric damage. It's simply suboptimal to not go for electric upgrades when presented, since I have built in electric and know for a fact I'll get upgrades for it. That's lame as hell, my build is literally locked in from the moment I choose my class. Like sure I CAN do something else but the only reason to do so is to be a contrarian. On top of every upgrade being extremely weaksauce I have ALWAYS felt like I know which one of the three presented is good for me to take (except when none of them are, which is like 30% of the time). It's always stupid obvious which upgrade works with your current build. And since the individual upgrades are all so weak, and rely heavily on synergies on top of synergies to meaningfully change your gameplay, there's no room to multibuild two different gimmicks or elements or anything. If you have a build that lets you stun, you take the extra damage to stunned enemies. If you have the fire damage, you take the enemies killed by fire leaving more fire. Since your other options will be like "Gain Stone Skin (temp overshield) when killing frozen enemies" (you have no way to freeze, your teammate has a cryo nade so that's why it's even offered) and "Heal like 2 hp when melee killing a big enough baddie". Please please please devs, make the runs actually fun and buff the ♥♥♥♥ out of all the upgrades. I wanna be able to spring around the caves at mach 10 with a speed build and then pick up something crazy that lets me deal more damage the faster I'm moving. I wanna be able to build melee and melee block and become a crazed pickaxer chewing through swarms with no ammo required and minimal damage taken (which I recover with vampire perks). I wanna be able to upgrade my class abilities enough for them to actually feel like a win button, and I want those class abilities to be more customizable or alterable in some way (at least let me pick a different element for my Falcon to use or something, it can function the same otherwise). I get that part of the design of this game it's that it's "harder" deep rock but it can be both fun and hard. If the upgrades are actually powerful, then as designers you can make the enemies way more plentiful or more powerful as you get lower into the caves and just build in some expectation that the players are making sensible build choices and will have something good set up by the time they have to face those challenges that would be insurmountable by an unupgraded dward (even a very skilled unupgraded dwarf). I hate the fact that right now an upgradeless run would feel SO do-able even as a newcomer to this game (with hundred of hours in OG DRG to be fair but still). Late game without upgrades should feel insane, because y'know... you're supposed to have upgrades that let you deal with the increased load. Instead it just feels the same but now I'm thinking harder about getting weakspot hits cause I deal 50% more weakspot damage to enemies under 50% health and have a 30% chance to crit when hitting weakspots and if that procs then I get 1.5 seconds of stun YIPPEEEEE SO IMPACTFUL.

TL;DR: I like the game, it's worth the price and then some, it's not perfect but I can see it getting close to perfection through early access. Remember DRG started out super bare-bones. I started playing DRG back in the early days, a couple of weeks after it released into early access on Steam. It was extremely charming, if slightly bare-bones, and I managed to sink about 150 hours into the game across early access. Every time an update rolled out, the game got better and better, more complex and with all sorts of new mechanics. I have every faith that the same thing will happen with Rogue Core. There are things that could be improved - cave layouts can get repetitive, there are obviously bugs (although no Glyphids that I've seen), and once you've played several runs you generally know what to expect from the mission. But overall, the core of the game, if you'll excuse the pun, is very solid, especially after the first patch completely overhauled the way that upgrades work. It rewards teamwork and cooperation and it rewards learning the classes and various upgrade systems so that you can figure out useful builds. And even if you have to pivot your build mid-run because you took [i]one[/i] poison upgrade and now every round of upgrades is all poison-based, generally speaking, it's still [i]fun[/i] to work around it. All of the classes have a unique feeling to them that makes it feel worthwhile to at least learn the basics, and if you want to be a better teammate, it's useful to familiarize yourself with their strengths and weaknesses. There is genuinely an impressive amount of depth to the bio-booster decks being mixed and matched across classes after promotion that lets you broaden your horizons or focus on something more specific. My current problems with the game lie mostly in the overall lack of variety, which is to be expected from an early access game where they're busy making sure the core mechanics work before branching out to new things. There is the aforementioned issue of taking an elemental upgrade and now having half your future upgrades based around that element. The cosmetic tree is somewhat lacking in interesting choices. And I do get tired of seeing the one cave generation that's got a tube of rock right through the middle of a big hollow space, with one easy-to-miss room tucked to the right of the cave entrance. But these are all things that will be ironed out over time as GSG adds more content in general. As of right now, I think the game is in a solid state, completely playable and enjoyable solo or co-op, for more than enough time to justify the price.

It's almost like the developers are going out of their way to ignore good suggestions and implement bad ones out of spite. I had hope with the first update that things were trending in the right direction, but after what they've done with 1.2 I would actively discourage anyone from buying this game, period. For some background, I have played Deep Rock Galactic since the season 4 update, and have clocked almost 1800 hours of time in it (though some of that is idle time, but not sure how much). I regularly play the game on hazard level 5, and will sometimes add additional modifiers like extra bugs. Among my biggest problems with Rogue Core are with the boss fight designs and the "reaperworms." They already have their issues, but the recent update just took everything I didn't like about them, and cranked it up to 11. The bosses have either difficult weak points / hitboxes, poorly telegraphed attacks, overpowered attacks, or some combination of the three. There could be other issues, but those are the ones that stand out to me. As for the reaperworms, I understand why they're there as a consequence for overstaying in a level; that said, having them be invulnerable AND capable of grabbing you without ANY way of mitigating or removing them to buy time or get some breathing room is absurd. As of the recent update, the developers have managed to somehow make them even worse (which I will elaborate on down below). GSG is taking a game that I really want to enjoy (as I think there is a lot of potential), and making it actively harder to like with almost every step they take. The developers responded to the bosses issue by giving them even MORE health (which they already had plenty of, considering how powerful builds can become by the endgame), and invulnerability phases, and even an ability to launch powerful counterattacks, making the fights even more unforgiving than they already are. And the cherry on top of this issue is that now the unique enemy spawn modifiers picked up throughout the run (Scorchers, Voidkin, etc.) now spawn IN THE BOSS'S arena while trying to fight them, making the fight complicated beyond what I think is reasonable. Basic creepers in the fight are one thing, but a large number of specials in the mix is way too much. The reaperworms, as I mentioned, are already a huge pain, for the reasons already mentioned above. The community has voiced their concerns on this, and the developers responded by making them even harder to lock down or keep at bay, more frequent and aggressive in their grabs, and (as a consequence of the change in spawn rate) multiple times more numerous. I understand that when the timer runs out you're meant to only survive a few minutes at the most under the increased pressure (incentivizing you to leave), but if any dwarf goes down, or anything else goes wrong for that matter, the team crumples almost immediately. These changes punish risk-taking far too harshly, and need to be reversed. There are better ways to make the worms punishing, but this definitely isn't it. I find a lot of enjoyment in playing solo from time to time, and in that regard Deep Rock Galactic was, in certain respects, more challenging to play than with other people. It did a good job of accounting for that however, and was still doable. Rogue Core, on the other hand, is an absolute nightmare to play solo. With the limited time (which with the timer changes is better, but still far from ideal), trying to manage resource collection, fight enemies, and do events by yourself is impossible in practice. Add on top of that the large swarms that are placed throughout the duration of time you have (in a given level), and you'll quickly find that you're constantly trying to "get ahead" of the enemy spawns. By the time you do (IF you do), you'll have run out of time and are (by way of unending swarms and reaper worms) forced to move on, if you can survive waiting for the elevator under pressure. Everything seems to be designed around having multiple people, and even then it can be a stretch to get everything. This part of the game design needs serious reworking with respect to solo play, and given the issues it currently has, I'm not holding my breath that it'll happen anytime soon. There are other issues here and there with the game in its current state, but they aren't egregious enough to warrant addressing right away. What I've laid out here, though, absolutely must be changed if I'm to consider playing this game any further, let alone recommending to anyone else. I actually tried to refund this game once because of how frustrated I was with it, and would probably do so now if I could. That, however, is unfortunately out of the question, given Steam's refund policy. All I can do now is vehemently recommend against purchasing to anyone still considering it until things change. I'll keep up with the game's development and change my review if things turn around, but until then I intend to avoid playing it, and I suggest you avoid it as well.

It has a different focus and is meant to be more challenging. After playing it for a while, the original almost feels like the vanilla version. The enemies are far more dangerous and genuinely creepy. Every run feels different thanks to the many combinations of perks, characters, weapons and equipment. I also like the stronger focus on survival. You have to decide whether you still have time to collect resources or start a minigame without risking the whole mission. These minigames give you useful upgrades for your current build instead of meaningless grind points, so they actually feel worth doing. There are still crashes, server problems and other stability issues, but the game isn’t finished yet and already has huge potential. I personally enjoy it even more than the original. I can't in good faith recommend this game. As an avid roguelike obsessive and someone with hundreds of hours in DRG, I was incredibly excited for this game. Initial reviews weren't great so I waited until after the first big patch. This game is insanely hard, but it never feels like its hard in a way that I can improve on. Even on the lowest "cautious" difficulty, i am running out of ammo on the 2nd or 3rd floor, in the midst of 5+ minutes of pure combat, and then i hear a "swarm incoming" message as I watch my corpse be danced on by 30+ enemies after i just killed over a hundred. There is no time for exploration, not enough ammo, and an incredible array of "feel bad" mechanics that make me want to play less with each inevitable and horrific loss. I have watched videos to see what I'm missing, but it seems I'm already using the "meta builds" which are still outright useless if your weapon isn't exactly perfect. Very rarely do I die and feel that I had any opportunity to survive. This game genuinely feels like it's punishing me for playing, and the upsides of the exceedingly rare victory are entirely negligible. I may pick this game up again in the future, but for now it'll be back to DRG until this game actually is balanced and enjoyable. I don't expect Danger 1 levels of ease, but I DO expect to feel like a loss is something I could have possibly prevented.
